issues.legal_issue: Collecting a duty linked to the production or manufacture of rubber from manufacturers who use the rubber does not make the levy constitutionally incompetent.
material_facts: The manufacturers used rubber in making chappals, although rubber constituted only part of the materials used.
The amended law permitted collection of the duty from either rubber-estate owners or manufacturers who used rubber.
The challenge argued that a duty collected from users fell outside the constitutional entry concerning duties on goods manufactured or produced in India.
issues.conclusion: The levy was within Parliament’s legislative competence. Collection from manufacturers was a method of collection and did not change the essential nature of a duty on production or manufacture; even if the levy did not qualify as an excise duty, Parliament had residual legislative competence to provide for its collection from users.
issues.legal_principle: Under Entry 84 of List I, an excise duty may be collected at a convenient stage, and the method of collection does not alter the essential nature of the tax so long as its connection with production or manufacture remains. Re: The Central Provinces and Berar Act, 14 of 1938 and R.C. Jall v. Union of India were applied. Independently, Entry 97 of List I read with Article 248 gives Parliament residual competence to legislate on a tax outside the enumerated entries.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax_levy: A party challenges the legislative competence to impose or collect a tax.
predicates.tax_linked_to_domestic_production: The tax is imposed in connection with goods produced or manufactured domestically.
predicates.collection_from_downstream_user: The law provides for collecting the tax from a person who uses the goods after their production or manufacture.
predicates.parliament_has_legislative_competence: Parliament has legislative competence to impose or provide for collection of the tax.

issues.definition: When a tax is linked to domestic production and is collected from a downstream user, a constitutional challenge to the tax does not prevent Parliament from having legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: Delegating the choice of collection category to an administrative body is not excessive when the enactment supplies a policy and the body is subject to meaningful safeguards and control.
material_facts: The law authorized the Board to collect the duty from either rubber-estate owners or manufacturers who used rubber, in accordance with rules made by the Central Government.
The statute stated the purpose of developing the rubber industry and provided for a Board representing producing interests, manufacturers, labour, and others.
The Board’s actions were subject to Central Government control.
The rules had to be placed before both Houses of Parliament, which could modify or annul them.

The Board was responsible for collecting the duty, and the legislative materials described difficulties in collecting it from numerous estate owners and the relative ease of collecting it from manufacturers.
issues.conclusion: The delegation was not excessive, and the statutory arrangement did not amount to an abdication of legislative functions.
issues.legal_principle: Essential legislative functions, including determining legislative policy, cannot be delegated, but subordinate legislation needed to implement a sufficiently clear policy may be delegated where guidance and safeguards exist. Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Birla Cotton, Spinning and Weaving Mills was followed. The Court also referred to M.M. Ipoh v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Raghubar Dayal Jai Prakash v. Union of India in considering guided administrative choice.

rule.if: excessive_delegation_challenge and enactment_states_public_policy and choice_limited_to_defined_categories and delegated_body_is_subject_to_oversight and rules_are_subject_to_legislative_review

predicates.excessive_delegation_challenge: A party challenges a law on the ground that it delegates legislative power excessively.
predicates.enactment_states_public_policy: The enactment states the public purpose that the delegated power is meant to serve.
predicates.choice_limited_to_defined_categories: The enactment confines the delegate’s choice to specified categories of persons from whom collection may be made.
predicates.delegated_body_is_subject_to_oversight: The delegate’s actions are subject to control by a government authority.
predicates.rules_are_subject_to_legislative_review: Rules made under the enactment must be presented to the legislature, which may review and change them.
predicates.delegation_is_not_excessive: The delegation is not invalid as an excessive delegation of legislative power.

issues.definition: A delegation challenged as excessive is not excessive when the enactment states its policy, confines the choice, and subjects the delegate and its rules to oversight.

issues.legal_issue: A guided choice between categories for collecting a levy does not violate equality when the choice serves a legitimate collection purpose and is constrained against arbitrary discrimination.
material_facts: The law permitted collection from either estate owners or manufacturers who used rubber.
Collection from estate owners had been difficult because there were many estates and some owners failed to register or submit accurate returns.
The legislative materials stated that collecting from the smaller number of manufacturers would be easier and would improve collection.
The rules and statutory safeguards governed the choice, and the Board was subject to Central Government control.
issues.conclusion: The statutory discretion did not violate Article 14; the Board could not arbitrarily discriminate between owners and manufacturers or among persons within either category.
issues.legal_principle: For an Article 14 challenge to administrative choice, the Court considered whether the enactment’s policy and safeguards guided the choice and whether the distinction served the collection objective. The factual material in a statement of objects and reasons may be considered in assessing an alleged Article 14 infringement. M.M. Ipoh v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Raghubar Dayal Jai Prakash v. Union of India were referred to.

predicates.equality_challenge_to_collection_discret: A party challenges discretion to choose between categories of persons for collection as unequal treatment.
predicates.collection_problems_differ_between_categ: The practical difficulty of collecting from one category differs from the difficulty of collecting from another category.
predicates.choice_advances_effective_collection: Choosing between the categories is directed at making collection more effective.
predicates.discretion_is_guided_and_reviewable: The choice is governed by statutory guidance and is subject to oversight or review.
predicates.collection_discretion_does_not_violate_e: The collection discretion does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.

issues.definition: A choice between collection categories does not violate equality when different collection difficulties justify the choice and the discretion is guided and reviewable.

issues.legal_issue: The rules identify manufacturers as the persons from whom the duty is collectible when they provide for a demand and recovery procedure against manufacturers but none against estate owners.
material_facts: The rules required manufacturers to submit returns concerning rubber acquired and used in manufacture and also contained provisions concerning returns and assessment for owners.
Rule 33D provided for a demand notice to a manufacturer and required payment by the manufacturer.
Rule 33D provided for steps to recover an unpaid amount from a manufacturer as arrears of land revenue.
The rules did not prescribe a corresponding demand or coercive recovery procedure against estate owners.
issues.conclusion: Read together, Rules 33, 33A and 33D made a definite provision that collection of the duty was to be made from manufacturers.
issues.legal_principle: The rules must be read together with the relevant provisions of section 12. Although returns and assessment could concern both owners and manufacturers, Rule 33D supplied the demand and recovery mechanism only for manufacturers; that scheme identified manufacturers as the category liable for collection.

predicates.challenge_to_clarity_of_collection_rules: A party challenges whether rules clearly identify the persons from whom a levy is collectible.
predicates.rules_provide_demand_against_manufacture: The rules require a formal demand for payment to be made to manufacturers.
predicates.rules_provide_recovery_against_manufactu: The rules authorize recovery from manufacturers when they do not pay after demand.
predicates.no_corresponding_owner_collection_proced: The rules contain no corresponding demand and coercive recovery procedure against owners.
predicates.manufacturers_are_the_collection_categor: Manufacturers are the category from whom the levy is collectible under the rules.

issues.definition: When a clarity challenge concerns collection rules that provide demand and recovery against manufacturers but no corresponding procedure against owners, the rules identify manufacturers as the collection category.
